addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- code-assist: This sop guides the implementation of code tasks using test-driven development principles, following a structured Explore, Plan, Code, Commit workflow. It balances automation with user collaboration while adhering to existing package patterns and prioritizing readability and extensibility. The agent acts as a Technical Implementation Partner and TDD Coach - providing guidance, generating test cases and implementation code that follows existing patterns, avoids over-engineering, and produces idiomatic, modern code in the target language.
- code-task-generator: This SOP generates structured code task files from rough descriptions, ideas, PDD implementation plans, or Intropy shaping packages. It automatically detects the input type and creates properly formatted code task files following the code task format specification. For PDD plans, it processes implementation steps one at a time to allow for learning and adaptation between steps. For shaping packages, it generates an implementation plan from the shaped design and then produces tasks from the approved plan. When the work involves scaffolding a new project, it emits a dedicated scaffold task that uses the `intropy` CLI to generate the project skeleton before any implementation begins.
- codebase-summary: This sop analyzes a codebase and generates comprehensive documentation including structured metadata files that describe the system architecture, components, interfaces, and workflows. It can create targeted documentation files like AGENTS.md (README for AI agents), README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, or generate a complete documentation ecosystem. The documentation is organized to make it easy for AI assistants to understand the system and help with development tasks.

Use this skill whenever the user mentions .NET tests, xUnit, test quality, test review, test improvements, test coverage analysis, TDD in C#, or asks to review or improve unit tests in a .NET codebase — even if they don't explicitly say "TDD" or "test-driven development". Also trigger when the user shares C# test files and wants feedback, or when they ask about testing patterns, mocking strategies, or test naming conventions in .NET.

This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

Use when building, modifying, or reviewing a Go CLI tool — especially for command structure, flag handling, configuration layering, version embedding, exit codes, I/O patterns, signal handling, shell completion, argument validation, and CLI unit testing. Also triggers when code uses cobra, viper, or urfave/cli.

Also use when performing performance code review to suggest improvements or benchmarks that could help identify quick performance gains. Not for measurement methodology (see golang-benchmark skill) or debugging workflow (see golang-troubleshooting skill).

Use this skill whenever someone asks to create golden path documentation, scaffold a TechDocs tutorial, write onboarding docs for a new integration pattern, document a Blueprint or Block, or set up step-by-step developer guides for Backstage. Use this skill whenever someone asks to add a new infrastructure component, deploy a new Helm chart to the service plane, set up a new platform service, onboard a new operator or tool to the cluster, or scaffold GitOps manifests for a service. 1	// Package blueprint downloads, validates, describes, and renders Intropy blueprints.
2	//
3	// A blueprint is a template.yaml manifest plus a skeleton/ directory. The
4	// package supports two main workflows:
5	//   - Describe: fetch a blueprint manifest and return its metadata and parameters.
6	//   - Create: fetch a blueprint, resolve parameter values, and render files.
7	//
8	// Create also writes a scaffold record (.intropy/scaffold.json) into the
9	// output directory, pinning the blueprint, version, and resolved values.
10	//
11	// A blueprint may additionally carry a manifests/ directory — a second
12	// template.yaml + skeleton/ pair with the same contract — holding Kubernetes
13	// deployment manifest templates. It is consumed by the deploy package
14	// (`intropy manifests create`), which re-fetches the pinned version from the
15	// scaffold record and renders manifests/skeleton with values seeded from the
16	// record.
17	package blueprint

content.content:
1	// Package deploy generates Kubernetes deployment manifests (a kustomize
2	// base + overlays tree) for a previously scaffolded integration. It reads
3	// the committed .intropy/scaffold.json record, re-fetches the exact
4	// blueprint version it pins, and renders the blueprint's manifests/
5	// directory with the blueprint package's template machinery.
6	package deploy
7	
8	import (
9		"context"
10		"encoding/json"
11		"errors"
12		"fmt"
13		"io"
14		"net/http"
15		"os"
16		"path/filepath"
17	
18		"github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/internal/blueprint"
19	)
20	
21	const (
22		// manifestDirName is the directory inside a blueprint (next to
23		// skeleton/) that holds the deployment manifest template:
24		// <blueprint>/manifests/template.yaml + <blueprint>/manifests/skeleton/.
25		manifestDirName = "manifests"
26	
27		templateManifestName = "template.yaml"
28		skeletonDirName      = "skeleton"
29	
30		// scaffoldValuesKey is the reserved key under which the full scaffold
31		// value map is exposed to manifest templates ({{ .scaffold.name }}).
32		scaffoldValuesKey = "scaffold"
33	
34		// defaultOutputDirName is the output directory relative to the project
35		// root when --output is not given.
36		defaultOutputDirName = "deploy"
37	)
38	
39	type CreateOptions struct {
40		StartDir   string // directory to begin the scaffold.json walk-up from; default "."
41		OutputDir  string // default <projectRoot>/deploy
42		Version    string // blueprint release tag; default: the tag pinned in scaffold.json
43		SetValues  map[string]any
44		Files      []string
45		Force      bool
46		NoInput    bool
47		OutputJSON string // path to write CreateResult JSON; "-" means stdout
48		Stdin      io.Reader
49		Stdout     io.Writer
50		Stderr     io.Writer
51		HTTP       *http.Client
52		UserAgent  string
53	
54		// Test overrides. Production callers leave these zero-valued; the
55		// blueprint is fetched from the owner/repo recorded in scaffold.json.
56		Owner         string
57		Repo          string
58		GitHubBaseURL string
59	}
60	
61	// CreateResult is the machine-readable summary written when --output-json is
62	// set. Field names are stable and additive-only.
63	type CreateResult struct {
64		Blueprint string         `json:"blueprint"`
65		Owner     string         `json:"owner"`
66		Repo      string         `json:"repo"`
67		Version   string         `json:"version"`
68		OutputDir string         `json:"outputDir"`
69		Values    map[string]any `json:"values"`
70	}
71	
72	func (o *CreateOptions) applyDefaults() {
73		if o.StartDir == "" {
74			o.StartDir = "."
75		}
76		if o.Stdin == nil {
77			o.Stdin = os.Stdin
78		}
79		if o.UserAgent == "" {
80			o.UserAgent = "intropy-cli"
81		}
82	}
83	
84	// Create generates the deployment manifests: locate scaffold.json, download
85	// the pinned blueprint, load manifests/template.yaml, resolve values (seeded
86	// from the scaffold record, with optional interactive prompting), render
87	// manifests/skeleton into the output directory.
88	func Create(ctx context.Context, opts CreateOptions) error {
89		opts.applyDefaults()
90	
91		scaffold, projectRoot, err := blueprint.FindScaffold(opts.StartDir)
92		if err != nil {
93			if errors.Is(err, blueprint.ErrScaffoldNotFound) {
94				return fmt.Errorf("%w\nThis project was scaffolded before deployment metadata existed. Re-scaffold it with 'intropy int create', or commit a minimal %s:\n  {\"schemaVersion\":1,\"blueprint\":\"<blueprint>\",\"owner\":\"integrio-intropy\",\"repo\":\"intropy-blueprints\",\"version\":\"<tag>\",\"values\":{\"name\":\"<name>\"}}", err, blueprint.ScaffoldRelPath)
95			}
96			return err

content.text:
`template.yaml` is the manifest half of a blueprint — every blueprint in the `integrio-intropy/intropy-blueprints` repo is a `template.yaml` plus a `skeleton/` directory, and the CLI uses the manifest to know what parameters a blueprint takes and how to resolve them before rendering the skeleton. Three commands consume it:

**Loading and validation** (`internal/blueprint/manifest.go:144`): `LoadTemplate` parses the file into a `Template` struct with a Kubernetes/Backstage-style envelope (`apiVersion: intropy.dev/v1`, `kind: Template`, `metadata`, `spec`). Validation requires that exact apiVersion/kind, a `metadata.name`, and that `spec.parameters` is a JSON Schema of `type: object`. A custom `UnmarshalYAML` also captures the YAML declaration order of `spec.parameters.properties`, so prompts and describe output appear in the order the blueprint author wrote them.

**What the spec drives:**
- `spec.parameters` — a JSON Schema whose properties become `FieldSpec`s (`manifest.go:107`). These drive interactive prompting, `--set` type coercion, and final validation of the merged value map against the schema (`values.go:202`).
- `spec.values` — derived values: each entry is a Go text/template (with sprig) rendered against the resolved parameters and added to the value map (`values.go:135`). Keys colliding with parameter names are rejected.

**The three consumers:**

1. **`intropy int create`** (`internal/blueprint/create.go:121`): downloads the blueprint tarball, loads `<blueprint>/template.yaml`, then resolves values by layering — schema defaults → `--values` files (stdin via `-`) → `--set` flags → interactive prompts for missing required fields (skipped under `--no-input` or non-TTY). The merged map is schema-validated, derived values are rendered, and the result feeds `Render` over `skeleton/`. The resolved values are also pinned into `.intropy/scaffold.json`.

2. **`intropy int describe`** (`internal/blueprint/describe.go:79`): loads the same file just to report the blueprint's metadata and parameters (in declaration order) without rendering anything.

3. **`intropy manifests create`** (`internal/deploy/create.go:131`): a blueprint may carry a *second* template.yaml at `<blueprint>/manifests/template.yaml` with its own `skeleton/` — same contract, but holding Kubernetes deployment manifest templates. The deploy package re-fetches the version pinned in `scaffold.json`, loads that manifest, and resolves values via `ResolveLayered` with the scaffold record's values as a base layer (so they apply without re-prompting but still yield to explicit `--values`/`--set`).

So in short: template.yaml is never itself rendered — it's the contract that declares, validates, and derives the values that the templating engine then applies to the sibling `skeleton/` tree.

content.text:
Sure — the repo builds to `./bin/intropy` via `make build`, so you just point an alias at that path. Add this to your `~/.zshrc`:

```zsh
alias intropy-test="/Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli/bin/intropy"
```

Then reload with `source ~/.zshrc` (or open a new terminal).

Workflow:

```zsh
cd ~/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli
make build          # rebuilds ./bin/intropy with version metadata via ldflags
intropy-test version   # runs your local build
intropy version        # still runs the Homebrew install
```

The two never collide because the Homebrew binary lives on your `PATH` (e.g. `/opt/homebrew/bin/intropy`) while the alias resolves to the absolute path of the local build.

Two small notes:
- Aliases only work in interactive shells. If you need the test binary in scripts or tools that don't read your zshrc, use a symlink instead: `ln -s ~/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli/bin/intropy ~/bin/intropy-test` (assuming `~/bin` is on your PATH).
- If you want alias-and-rebuild in one step, you can make it a function instead: `intropy-test() { make -C ~/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli --quiet build && ~/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli/bin/intropy "$@" }` — always runs the freshest code, at the cost of a rebuild check per invocation.
